lessons.title: Persistent data structures
lessons.summary: How immutable lists, trees, maps and vectors make cheap "modified copies" by sharing structure, the 32-way tries behind Clojure, Scala and Immutable.js, and the traps where persistence breaks amortised bounds.
lessons.body:
Immutability has an obvious cost. If you can never change a list in place, then "add one element" seems to mean "copy the whole list and add one element". Do that in a loop over a million items and you've written an O(n²) algorithm.

Efficient persistent collections reduce that cost through sharing. **Persistence** means: every "update" returns a new version, the old version stays valid, and the two **share almost all of their memory**. Only the small part that actually changed is new.

This lesson shows how that works, from the humble linked list up to the 32-way tries that power Clojure's vectors and maps, and where the trick stops being free.

## What "persistent" means

Here *persistent* has nothing to do with disks. It means old versions persist after an update.

| Kind | Old versions can be |
|---|---|
| Ephemeral (normal) | gone after update |
| Partially persistent | read, not updated |
| Fully persistent | read and updated |
| Confluent | merged with each other |

Purely functional structures are fully persistent automatically: nothing is ever mutated, so every version you hold a reference to is still intact and can be the starting point of new updates.

The naive way to get this is to copy everything on every update. The real way is **structural sharing**.

## The linked list: sharing for free

The singly linked list (a *cons list*) is the simplest persistent structure. Each cell holds a value and a pointer to the rest:

```python
xs = (3, None)
ys = (2, xs)       # [2, 3]
a  = (1, ys)       # [1, 2, 3]
b  = (9, ys)       # [9, 2, 3]

a[1] is b[1]       # True: shared tail
```

```
a --> [1|*]--+
             v
           [2|*]--> [3|/]
             ^
b --> [9|*]--+
```

Prepending to a list allocates one cell and points it at the old list. It's O(1) time and space, and the old list is untouched. That's why Haskell, Lisp, Erlang and Elixir lists grow at the front.

The costs show up at the other end:

| Operation | Cost | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Prepend | O(1) | new head, shared tail |
| Head / tail | O(1) | follow one pointer |
| Append | O(n) | copy every cell |
| Index i | O(i) | walk i pointers |
| Update at i | O(i) | copy cells 0..i |

Appending must copy every cell, because the last cell's pointer has to change and every cell before it points (indirectly) at that one. For this immutable linked-list path-copying scheme, copy the prefix leading to the change; persistence in general has other implementation techniques.

## Trees: path copying

That rule gives the key technique for trees. To change a leaf of a tree, copy **only the nodes on the path from the root to it**. Every subtree off that path is reused by pointer.

Inserting 65 into a binary search tree:

```
version 1:
        50
       /  \
     30    70
    /  \   / \
   20  40 60  80

version 2 (after inserting 65):
        50'
       /  \
    (30)   70'
           / \
         60'  (80)
           \
            65
```

Nodes marked `'` are new copies, and 65 is the new leaf. `(30)` (with its whole subtree) and `(80)` are the very same objects as in version 1, reached by pointer. Here's the whole thing in Python:

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

class Node(NamedTuple):
    key: int
    left: "Node | None"
    right: "Node | None"

def insert(t, k):
    if t is None:
        return Node(k, None, None)
    if k < t.key:
        return t._replace(
            left=insert(t.left, k))
    if k > t.key:
        return t._replace(
            right=insert(t.right, k))
    return t
```

`_replace` builds a new node with one field changed. The new version shares the whole left subtree:

```python
v2 = insert(v1, 65)
v2.left is v1.left        # True
v2.right.right is v1.right.right  # True
```

For a **balanced** tree of n keys, the path has about log₂ n nodes. With a million keys that's about 20 new nodes per insert, instead of a million. Both versions remain fully usable, and the extra memory is O(log n) per update.

This is how Haskell's `Data.Map` and `Data.Set` (size-balanced binary trees), OCaml's `Map`, and Scala's `TreeMap` work. Rebalancing (rotations in a red-black or AVL tree) only touches nodes near the path, so it stays O(log n).

> [!example] Git does this too
> A Git commit points to a tree object for the root directory, which points to trees and blobs for its contents. Change one file and Git writes a new blob, new trees for each directory on the path up to the root, and a new commit. Every unchanged directory is shared with the previous commit by hash. That's path copying on your file system.

## Wide trees: the 32-way trie

A balanced binary tree can require about 20 dependent node accesses for a million keys; cache behavior depends on layout and workload. Wide tries reduce depth.

### Persistent vectors

Clojure's `PersistentVector` (designed by Rich Hickey, building on Phil Bagwell's work) uses internal nodes with up to **32 child slots**. To find index i, split i into 5-bit chunks (2⁵ = 32) and use each chunk to pick a child:

```
index 1000 = 0b 00000 11111 01000
               level0 level1 leaf
                0      31     8
```

Ignoring tail optimization and partially filled roots, the number of array levels is ceil(log₃₂ n):

| Elements | Levels |
|---|---|
| 32 | 1 |
| 1,024 | 2 |
| 32,768 | 3 |
| ~1 million | 4 |
| ~1 billion | 6 |

Six hops for a billion elements is why people call these operations "effectively constant". They are still O(log n), but the base is 32.

Updating index i uses path copying: copy each node on the path (each a 32-slot array) and change one slot. For a million-element vector that's 4 arrays of 32 pointers, about 1 KB at 8 bytes a pointer, versus 8 MB to copy the whole backing array.

One more trick makes appends fast. The vector keeps its last (up to) 32 elements in a separate **tail** array outside the tree. Most appends just copy that small tail; roughly once per 32 appends, a full tail is pushed into the tree when the next tail starts.

### Hash array mapped tries (HAMTs)

Maps and sets use the same shape keyed by hash. A common 32-way HAMT uses 5 hash bits per level. Bitmap nodes record occupied slots and compact their entries; implementations also use dense nodes and explicit hash-collision nodes. A child's position in the array is the number of set bits before its slot (a population-count operation, whose machine instructions depend on the target).

That compression matters: a sparse node with 3 children stores 3 pointers, not 32.

HAMTs are everywhere once you look:

- Clojure's `PersistentHashMap` and `PersistentHashSet`
- Scala's immutable `HashMap` and `HashSet`
- Immutable.js `Map` (its `List` is a vector trie)
- Erlang and Elixir maps with more than 32 keys
- CPython's `contextvars`, which uses a HAMT internally so that copying a context is cheap

## Why bother: what sharing buys you

### Cheap snapshots and undo

Retaining an old root is a cheap snapshot, but keeps its reachable nodes alive. An editor's undo stack is just a list of previous document values. A game can keep the last 60 frames of state for rewind with memory proportional to what changed.

### O(1) change detection

If two references point to the same object, nothing inside changed. React and Redux depend on this: `React.memo` compares each prop with `Object.is`, and Redux's `useSelector` compares results by reference, which is only correct if updates create new objects rather than mutating old ones. Many persistent APIs reuse identity for no-op updates, but that behavior is API-dependent; different references need not mean different contents.

### Safe sharing across threads

Deeply immutable data can avoid locks for its contents after safe publication and while its lifetime is guaranteed; mutable elements or reference-management protocols still need care. A Clojure atom holds a persistent value: a writer builds a new version and swaps a single pointer with compare-and-set, while readers keep using whatever version they grabbed.

## Where it gets hard

### Constant factors

A persistent vector lookup is several dependent pointer loads; an array lookup is one. Each update allocates fresh nodes, which means garbage collection pressure. For a tight numeric loop over a large array, a mutable array is typically much faster. Persistent collections win when you actually need old versions or sharing, not by default.

### Amortisation breaks under persistence

The classic functional queue keeps two lists: `front` for popping and `back` for pushing (newest first). When `front` runs out, reverse `back` into a new `front`:

```python
def push(q, x):
    front, back = q
    return front, (x, back)

def pop(q):
    front, back = q
    if front is None:
        while back is not None:
            x, back = back
            front = (x, front)
    if front is None:
        raise IndexError("empty queue")
    x, rest = front
    return x, (rest, back)
```

Each list is a nested (head, tail) tuple ending in None, as above; the empty queue is (None, None). Both prepend and tail access are O(1).

Used normally, each element is reversed once, so the costs average out to O(1) per operation. That's an **amortised** bound: occasional expensive reverses are paid for by many cheap pushes.

Persistence breaks the argument. Take a version `q` whose `front` is empty and whose `back` holds n items. If you call `pop(q)` a thousand times (on the *same* old version, which persistence explicitly allows), each call does the full O(n) reverse. The "savings" from cheap pushes were spent once, but the expensive step is replayed every time.

Chris Okasaki's fix, in *Purely Functional Data Structures*, is to combine persistence with **laziness**: arrange lazy memoized work so branches share a suspension created before they diverge. Creating a fresh thunk in each pop would still repeat the reversal. Appropriate invariants recover amortised bounds; incremental rotation and scheduling are additionally needed for worst-case O(1).

> [!warning] Rule of thumb
> If a persistent structure's docs say "amortised", check whether that bound holds when old versions are reused. Okasaki-style structures are designed for it; a naive port of a mutable algorithm usually isn't.

### Bulk builds and transients

Building a 100,000-element vector by 100,000 persistent appends creates 100,000 intermediate versions that nobody will ever look at. Libraries offer a controlled escape hatch:

- **Clojure transients**: `(persistent! (reduce conj! (transient []) xs))` uses an isolated transient, then returns a persistent value in O(1). Always capture the returned transient from each update and stop using it after persistent!.
- **Immutable.js** `withMutations`: batch updates on a temporary mutable copy.
- **Immer** (JavaScript): write ordinary mutating code against a draft; it produces a new immutable object that shares every untouched part with the original.

All three rely on the same insight: mutation is safe as long as no one else holds a reference to the thing being mutated.

### Python's options

In CPython, appending to a nonempty tuple with t + (x,) copies its references in O(n), while the elements themselves remain shared. This preserves the old tuple and is persistent in the semantic sense, but lacks an efficient tree-based update path. For real persistent collections, use a library such as `pyrsistent` (`pvector`, `pmap`, `pset`), or accept copying when the data is small.

## Key takeaways
- Persistent structures keep old versions valid; structural sharing is a technique for doing so efficiently.
- Cons lists share tails: prepend is O(1), but append and indexed update copy the prefix.
- Trees use path copying: copy the root-to-change path, O(log n) nodes, and reuse every other subtree.
- 32-way tries (vectors) and HAMTs (maps, sets) keep depth around 4 for a million items, making updates and lookups "effectively constant".
- Sharing gives cheap snapshot roots and useful identity checks; safe publication, deep immutability and lifetime management still govern concurrent reads.
- Costs are pointer chasing, allocation and GC; amortised bounds can break when old versions are reused, which Okasaki fixes with laziness.
- Transients, `withMutations` and Immer allow local mutation for bulk work, then freeze the result.

questions.prompt: In the phrase *persistent data structure*, what does "persistent" mean?

options.text: The data is saved to disk and survives a restart
options.explanation: That's the database meaning of persistence. Here it's about versions in memory, not storage.

options.text: Old versions remain valid and usable after an update
options.explanation: Correct. An update returns a new version, and anyone holding the previous version still sees it unchanged.

options.text: The structure can never be garbage collected
options.explanation: Old versions are collected normally once nothing references them. Persistence is about not *destroying* them on update.

options.text: Every update copies the entire structure
options.explanation: That would give persistence, but it's the naive approach. Real persistent structures share unchanged parts so updates are cheap.

questions.workedExample:
Compare with a normal (ephemeral) Python list:

```python
xs = [1, 2]
ys = xs
xs.append(3)
ys    # [1, 2, 3]: old
      # version is gone
```

With a persistent vector, `xs2 = xs.append(3)` returns a new version, and `xs` is still `[1, 2]`. Structural sharing makes keeping both cheap.

questions.prompt: On an immutable singly linked (cons) list of n elements, which operations take O(1) time? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Allocate one cell pointing at the existing list; the old list is shared, untouched.
Correct. The head is stored in the first cell.

options.text: Getting the tail (everything but the first element)
options.explanation: Correct. The tail is just the first cell's pointer, already a complete list.

options.text: Appending an element at the end
options.explanation: The last cell's pointer must change, so every cell that leads to it must be copied: O(n).
There's no pointer to the end; you have to walk all n cells.

questions.workedExample:
Ask: does the operation touch only the first cell?

| Operation | Cells touched |
|---|---|
| prepend | 1 new |
| head | 1 |
| tail | 1 |
| append | n copied |
| last | n walked |

This is why functional code builds lists by prepending and, if order matters, reverses once at the end.

questions.prompt: In CPython, `t` is a tuple of 1,000,000 items. What does `t2 = t + (x,)` cost?

options.text: O(1), because tuples are immutable and share structure
options.explanation: Being immutable doesn't imply structural sharing. CPython tuples are flat arrays, so concatenation builds a new one.

options.text: O(n) time and memory: it copies all 1,000,000 references into a new tuple
options.explanation: Correct. Concatenation preserves the old tuple, so it is persistent in the semantic sense, but lacks an efficient path-copying layout. `pyrsistent`'s `pvector` would make this effectively constant.

options.text: O(log n), because Python uses path copying for tuples
options.explanation: Path copying needs a tree. A tuple is a single contiguous block of references.

options.text: It raises an error because tuples can't be changed
options.explanation: Concatenation doesn't change `t`; it creates a new tuple. That's allowed.

questions.workedExample:
1. A CPython tuple stores its items in one contiguous array.
2. `t + (x,)` allocates a new array of 1,000,001 slots and copies every reference.
3. With 8-byte pointers that's about 8 MB copied for one append.

In a loop of n appends that's O(n²). Persistence does not require a tree or sharing; those are techniques for making versioned updates efficient.

questions.prompt: You insert one key into a persistent, nearly complete binary search tree (using path copying, ignoring rebalancing overhead) holding about 1,000,000 keys. Roughly how many new nodes are allocated?

options.explanation: Only true for prepending to a list. In a tree, the new leaf's parent changes, so it must be copied, and so must its parent, up to the root.
Correct. Path copying copies the nodes on the root-to-leaf path, about log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20, plus the new leaf. Rebalancing touches only nodes near that path.
√n has no role here. The number copied is the height of the tree.
That's copying the whole tree. Path copying shares every subtree off the path.

questions.workedExample:
1. A balanced tree with n keys has height about log₂ n.
2. log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 19.9, so about 20 levels.
3. Each node on the path needs a new copy with one child pointer changed.
4. All off-path subtrees are reused; the exact node count depends on tree shape and balancing work.

So each version costs about 20 nodes of extra memory, and old and new versions remain fully usable.

questions.prompt: `v1` is the 7-node tree from the lesson (root 50; 30 with children 20, 40; 70 with children 60, 80). After `v2 = insert(v1, 65)` with the path-copying `insert`, which are `True`? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. 65 > 50, so insertion goes right; the left subtree (30, 20, 40) is reused by pointer.
65 goes into 70's subtree, so node 70 is copied with a new left child. It's a different object.
Correct. 65 < 70, so the path goes left at 70; the 80 node is shared.
The root is always on the path, so it's always copied when a new key is inserted.
Correct. If the 30 subtree is shared, its child 20 is the same object too.

questions.workedExample:
Trace the path for 65:

```
50: 65 > 50, go right
70: 65 < 70, go left
60: 65 > 60, go right
None: create 65
```

Copied: 50, 70, 60 (plus the new 65). Shared: 30 and everything under it, and 80.

So anything reached through `.left` from the root, and `.right.right`, is the same object in both versions.

questions.prompt: A persistent vector uses a 32-way trie (ignore the tail optimisation). How many levels does it need for 30,000 elements?

options.explanation: Two levels hold at most 32² = 1,024 elements, far fewer than 30,000.
Correct. 32² = 1,024 is too few and 32³ = 32,768 is enough, so 3 levels.
That's roughly log₁₀ or a mix-up with the 5 bits per level. Each level consumes 5 bits of the index; 15 bits cover 32,768 indices.
15 is the number of index *bits* needed, not levels. Each level uses 5 of them.

questions.workedExample:
Each level multiplies capacity by 32:

| Levels | Capacity |
|---|---|
| 1 | 32 |
| 2 | 1,024 |
| 3 | 32,768 |

30,000 ≤ 32,768, so 3 levels. Equivalently log₃₂(30,000) ≈ 2.97, rounded up to 3.

In bits: indices 0 to 29,999 need 15 bits, and 15 / 5 = 3 levels.

questions.prompt: You update one element of a persistent vector of about 1,000,000 elements (a 4-level, 32-way trie, 8-byte pointers). Roughly how much new memory is allocated, compared with copying a flat array of 1,000,000 pointers?

options.explanation: Only one slot changes, but whole nodes are copied, not single slots; each node is a 32-pointer array.
Correct. 4 nodes on the path, each 32 pointers × 8 bytes = 256 bytes, so about 1,024 bytes. A full copy is 1,000,000 × 8 = 8 MB.
That would be copying about a thousand nodes. Path copying copies only the 4 on the path.
Path copying shares every node off the path, so it doesn't copy the whole vector.

questions.workedExample:
1. Depth: log₃₂(1,000,000) ≈ 4 levels.
2. Each level on the path gets a fresh 32-slot array: 32 × 8 = 256 bytes.
3. 4 × 256 = 1,024 bytes ≈ 1 KB (plus small per-object headers).
4. A flat copy: 1,000,000 × 8 bytes = 8 MB.

That's roughly 8,000 times less. The trade-off is that a lookup does 4 dependent pointer loads instead of 1.

questions.prompt: A plain Redux reducer, operating on unfrozen state outside Immer, does `state.items.push(item); return state;`. The store's state really does contain the new item, but components using `useSelector(s => s.items)` don't re-render. Why?

options.text: Redux batches updates and will re-render later
options.explanation: Batching delays work but doesn't drop it. That state update does not change the selected reference; unrelated updates can still render the component.

options.text: `useSelector` compares the selected value by reference; the mutated array is the same object, so it looks unchanged
options.explanation: Correct. Change detection by reference equality only works if every change produces a new object. Mutating in place defeats it.

options.text: `push` doesn't work on arrays inside objects
options.explanation: `push` worked; the state does contain the item. The problem is detecting that it changed.

options.text: Reducers must return `undefined` to trigger a re-render
options.explanation: Returning `undefined` from a reducer is an error in Redux. It must return the next state.

questions.workedExample:
1. Before and after the action, `s.items` is the **same array object**.
2. `useSelector` checks `prev === next`; that's `true`, so it concludes nothing changed.
3. No re-render.

The fix is a persistent-style update that creates new objects along the path to the change and shares the rest:

```javascript
return { ...state,
  items: [...state.items, item] };
```

Or use Immer (built into Redux Toolkit), which writes that for you from mutating-looking code.

questions.prompt: Using the lesson's two-list queue, `q` has an empty `front` and 1,000 items in `back`. A program calls `pop(q)` five times, **each time on the same `q`** (say, five branches of a search). How many element copies do the reversals do in total?

options.text: About 1,000, since the reversal cost is amortised
options.explanation: The amortised argument assumes each reversal happens once. Persistence lets you replay the expensive step from the same old version.
Correct. Every `pop(q)` sees the same empty `front` and reverses all 1,000 items again: 5 × 1,000.

options.text: About 5, since each pop is O(1)
options.explanation: For the lesson's cons-list implementation, pop is O(1) when front is nonempty. Here it's empty every time, because `q` itself never changes.

options.text: About 1,000,000, because each pop reverses n² items
options.explanation: A single reverse is O(n), not O(n²): 1,000 copies each.

questions.workedExample:
1. `pop(q)` finds `front` empty, so it reverses 1,000 items to make a new front.
2. It returns a **new** queue; `q` is untouched (that's persistence).
3. The next `pop(q)` sees the same empty `front` and does it again.
4. 5 calls × 1,000 = 5,000 copies.

Used linearly (always popping from the latest version), the first pop pays 1,000 and the next ones are O(1). Appropriate lazy-queue designs arrange shared suspensions before version branches diverge, so expensive work is not recomputed. Simply creating a fresh thunk in each pop would not fix this.

questions.prompt: A HAMT node has the bitmap `0b10110` (bit 0 is the rightmost) and a compact child array. A lookup's 5 hash bits select slot 4. Which array index holds that child?

options.explanation: That would be true in an uncompressed 32-slot array. The compact array only stores occupied slots, so you count set bits instead.
Correct. Bits 1, 2 and 4 are set. Slots 1 and 2 come before slot 4, so the child is at array index 2.
That's the total number of set bits. The index is the number of set bits *below* slot 4.
Bit 4 is set (0b1_0110), so the slot is occupied. An absent slot would have its bit clear.

questions.workedExample:
1. Bitmap `0b10110`: bits set at positions 1, 2, 4.
2. Check bit 4 is set: yes, so a child exists.
3. Mask off bits at or above 4: `0b10110 & 0b01111 = 0b00110`.
4. `popcount(0b00110) = 2`, so it's array index 2.

```
slot:  4 3 2 1 0
bit:   1 0 1 1 0
array: [s1, s2, s4]
index:   0   1   2
```

Population count has efficient hardware support on many targets, but generated instructions and cost vary; compression is not free.

questions.prompt: Which of these uses of local mutation inside a persistent-data codebase are safe? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inside a function, build a 100,000-element Clojure vector with a transient and `conj!`, then call `persistent!` before returning it
options.explanation: Correct. Keep the transient isolated, capture each update's returned transient, and stop using it after persistent! returns the persistent value in O(1).

options.text: Mutating a vector that is already stored in an atom other threads read from
options.explanation: Readers hold references to that value and assume it never changes. Mutating it breaks every one of them.

options.text: Using Immer's `produce` to push to a draft array in a reducer
options.explanation: Correct. You mutate a draft proxy; Immer produces a new immutable object that shares untouched parts with the original.

options.text: Calling `persistent!` on a transient and then continuing to `conj!` onto the same transient
options.explanation: After `persistent!` the transient is invalidated; Clojure throws if you keep using it, precisely because the frozen vector may share its nodes.

options.text: Batching updates with Immutable.js `withMutations` on a freshly created map
options.explanation: Correct. The temporary mutable copy is private until `withMutations` returns the immutable result.

questions.workedExample:
The test for every case: **can anyone else hold a reference to the thing being mutated?**

| Case | Shared? | Safe |
|---|---|---|
| transient, then `persistent!` | no | yes |
| mutate value in atom | yes | no |
| Immer draft | no | yes |
| reuse after `persistent!` | yes | no |
| `withMutations` | no | yes |

Persistent structures rely on old versions never changing. Mutation is fine as long as no old version can observe it.

questions.prompt: You build a list of n results in Haskell. Version A does `acc ++ [x]` for each item; version B does `x : acc` and calls `reverse` once at the end. What are their total costs?

options.explanation: `++` must copy its whole left argument, which is the growing accumulator, so A is not linear.

options.text: A is O(n²); B is O(n)
options.explanation: Correct. Each append in A copies the accumulator (1 + 2 + ... + n cells), while each prepend in B is O(1) and the single reverse is O(n).

options.text: A is O(n); B is O(n log n)
options.explanation: Neither prepending nor reversing a list involves a log factor; B is linear.

options.text: A is O(n log n); B is O(n²)
options.explanation: This is backwards. Prepending shares the old list; appending copies it.

questions.workedExample:
A: the k-th append copies the existing k - 1 cells:

```
0 + 1 + 2 + ... + (n - 1)
= n(n - 1) / 2  ->  O(n²)
```

For n = 100,000 that's about 5 billion cell copies.

B: n prepends at O(1) each, plus one reverse at O(n): O(n) total, about 200,000 steps.

It's the cons list's cost table in action: prepend shares the tail, append copies everything before the end.
